NaviGATE: Noise-Aware Dual-View Generation for
Multimodal Knowledge Graph Reasoning

Jie Peng    Yongxue Shan    Yongfu Zha    Cui Miao    Xiaodong Wang
Abstract

Multimodal knowledge graph reasoning (MKGR) aims to infer missing facts by jointly exploiting relational structures, textual descriptions, and visual evidence. Existing embedding-based methods effectively capture graph topology, but their fixed multimodal representations are less effective for query-specific fine-grained semantic reasoning, while generation-based methods are vulnerable to noisy retrieval and may produce invalid entities. To address these challenges, we propose NaviGATE, a noise-aware generative framework for MKGR. NaviGATE first aligns graph-derived structural representations with textual semantics, then performs structure-aware internal knowledge activation by fine-tuning the multimodal language model with multimodal entity summaries and injected structural tokens. In the noise-aware dual-view instruction tuning stage, NaviGATE jointly optimizes retrieval-free and retrieval-aware views: reliable retrieved candidates are reinforced through contrastive logit sharpening, while misleading candidates are suppressed through parametric consistency distillation. In inference, structure-constrained decoding restricts generation to valid entities in the target knowledge graph. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that NaviGATE consistently outperforms strong unimodal, multimodal, and generation-based baselines, and remains robust under noisy retrieval scenarios.

Introduction

Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) integrate structured relational facts with multimodal information, such as textual descriptions and visual images, and have become important knowledge resources for artificial intelligence applications, including recommendation systems (Xian et al. 2019; Kim et al. 2024), question answering (Li et al. 2020), and information retrieval (Li et al. 2024; Kim et al. 2025). However, real-world knowledge graphs are often incomplete, with many valid facts missing from the observed graph. Multimodal knowledge graph reasoning (MKGR) aims to predict missing entities by jointly exploiting graph structure and entity-associated multimodal context, and has attracted increasing attention in recent years.

Existing MKGR methods can be broadly categorized into embedding-based and generation-based approaches. Embedding-based methods encode entities, relations, and multimodal attributes into continuous representation spaces, and predict missing facts by scoring candidate triples. With graph neural networks (Li et al. 2023; Peng et al. 2025), translation-based constraints (Jian et al. 2025; Li et al. 2026), or multimodal fusion modules (Zhang et al. 2024a; Zhang et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2024c), these methods effectively preserve structural topology and enrich entity representations with textual and visual evidence. However, their dependence on fixed multimodal representations and predefined scoring functions limits their ability to perform query-specific fine-grained semantic reasoning. As a result, when multiple candidates are semantically similar, embedding-based models may narrow down the search space but remain insufficient to distinguish the exact target entity.

Generation-based methods (Yang et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2024b) offer a promising alternative by formulating MKGR as a text generation problem. Leveraging the semantic understanding and parametric knowledge of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), these methods can generate missing entities from textualized queries and multimodal contexts. Compared with embedding-based models, they provide greater flexibility in contextual reasoning and can better exploit relation semantics, entity descriptions, and visual information. Nevertheless, direct generation may produce answers that are not valid entities in the target knowledge graph or are inconsistent with the graph schema, which limits their completion performance. Recent retrieval-augmented frameworks (Liu et al. 2025a; Wei et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2025b) mitigate this issue by using an embedding-based retriever to obtain a top-K candidate set, which is then provided to the MLLM for reranking or generation. By combining structural recall with semantic reasoning, these methods have achieved notable performance improvements. However, this pipeline is fundamentally constrained by retriever recall: if the ground-truth entity is absent from the top-K candidate set, MLLMs may fail to reliably generate the correct answer; meanwhile, feeding the entire entity set into the model is impractical due to their limited context windows and attention budgets.

In realistic MKGR scenarios, retrieved candidates are not always reliable, since the ground-truth entity may be absent from the candidate set, making the retrieved candidate set noisy. Over-reliance on retrieval may force the generator to select an incorrect entity from the candidate set. This raises a key challenge: how can a generative MKGR model rely on retrieved evidence when it is reliable, while falling back on the LLM’s internal knowledge when the retrieved candidate set is noisy?

To address this challenge, we propose NaviGATE, a progressively optimized generative framework for MKGR. First, structure-semantic collaborative alignment coordinates structural entity representations with textual semantics in a shared space, enabling graph-derived knowledge to be integrated into the MLLM. Second, structure-aware internal knowledge activation trains the model with multimodal entity summaries and structural cues under a retrieval-free view, preserving its basic completion ability when retrieval is noisy. Third, noise-aware dual-view instruction tuning jointly optimizes retrieval-free and retrieval-aware predictions: reliable candidates are strengthened through contrastive logit sharpening, while misleading candidates are suppressed through parametric consistency distillation. During inference, structure-constrained decoding restricts outputs to valid KG entities. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose structure-semantic collaborative alignment and internal knowledge activation to inject graph-derived knowledge into the MLLM, building retrieval-free completion ability as a reliable fallback under noisy retrieval.

  • •

    We introduce noise-aware dual-view instruction tuning, which strengthens reliable candidates via contrastive logit sharpening and suppresses misleading ones via parametric consistency distillation. Structure-constrained decoding further ensures valid entity generation.

  • •

    Experiments on MKG-W and DB15K show that NaviGATE achieves the best MRR and Hits@1 among fifteen baselines and remains robust under noisy retrieval.

Related Work

Embedding-based knowledge graph reasoning

Embedding-based knowledge graph reasoning (KGR) learns entity and relation representations and predicts missing facts by scoring candidate triples. Classical models, such as TransE (Bordes et al. 2013a), DistMult (Yang et al. 2015), ComplEx (Trouillon et al. 2016), RotatE (Sun et al. 2019), and TuckER (Balazevic et al. 2019), mainly exploit structural triples to model relational patterns. MKGR methods further incorporate images and textual descriptions into entity representation learning, including IKRL (Xie et al. 2017), RSME (Wang et al. 2021), OTKGE (Cao et al. 2022), IMF (Li et al. 2023), QEB (Wang et al. 2023), VISTA (Lee et al. 2023), NativE (Zhang et al. 2024a), MyGO (Zhang et al. 2025), and APKGR (Jian et al. 2025). These methods improve structural retrieval through modality fusion, interaction, adaptive learning, or noise modeling, but still rely on fixed representations and predefined scoring functions. As fine-grained multimodal clues are compressed before inference, their query-specific reasoning ability remains limited when candidates are semantically similar.

Generation-based knowledge graph reasoning

Generation-based KGR formulates link prediction as a text generation task, where a generative language model produces the missing entity from a textualized query. Early methods, such as GenKGR (Xie et al. 2022) and KG-S2S (Yang et al. 2025), convert triples into natural language sequences and apply sequence-to-sequence models for entity generation. With the emergence of large language models, recent studies further explore instruction tuning, in-context learning, and retrieval-augmented generation for KGR. For instance, KG-LLM (Shu et al. 2025) and KoPA (Zhang et al. 2024b) finetunes LLMs on KG completion instructions, while KICGPT (Wei et al. 2023), SAT (Liu et al. 2025b), and DIFT (Liu et al. 2025a) combine embedding-based retrieval with LLM-based reranking or finetuning. These methods demonstrate the potential of language models in leveraging semantic priors for KGR. Nevertheless, they often remain sensitive to retrieval quality. When retrieved candidates are noisy or the ground-truth entity is absent, generation models can be misled by irrelevant evidence. Moreover, directly generated answers may not always correspond to valid entities in the KG. In contrast, our framework targets multimodal KGR by combining noise-aware dual-view instruction tuning with structure-constrained inference, achieving robust and valid entity generation under noisy multimodal retrieval.

Methodology

As shown in Figure 1, NaviGATE progressively performs structure-semantic collaborative alignment, retrieval-free internal knowledge activation, and noise-aware dual-view instruction tuning to exploit reliable candidates while mitigating misleading ones. Fin ally, structure-constrained decoding ensures valid entity generation.

Problem Formulation

We denote a multimodal knowledge graph as

𝒢=(ℰ,ℛ,𝒯,𝒟,ℐ),\mathcal{G}=\left(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{D},\mathcal{I}\right), (1)

where ℰ\mathcal{E} and ℛ\mathcal{R} denote the entity set and relation set, respectively. 𝒯={(h,r,t)∣h,t∈ℰ,r∈ℛ}\mathcal{T}=\{(h,r,t)\mid h,t\in\mathcal{E},r\in\mathcal{R}\} is the set of observed triples. Each entity e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E} may be associated with a textual description de∈𝒟d_{e}\in\mathcal{D} and a visual image ie∈ℐi_{e}\in\mathcal{I}. Given a query triple with one missing entity, MKGR aims to infer the missing entity from the entity set. Depending on whether the missing entity occurs in the tail or head position, the completion query can be formulated as (h,r,∗)(h,r,\ast) or (∗,r,t)(\ast,r,t), respectively, where ∗\ast denotes the unknown entity.

Unlike conventional embedding-based MKGR methods that score candidate triples with fixed representation functions, NaviGATE formulates MKGR as a constrained generation problem. Given the query context CqC_{q}, the model directly generates the surface name of the missing entity:

Pθ​(y∣Cq)=∏ℓ=1|Yy|Pθ​(Yy,ℓ∣Yy,<ℓ,Cq),P_{\theta}(y\mid C_{q})=\prod_{\ell=1}^{|Y_{y}|}P_{\theta}\left(Y_{y,\ell}\mid Y_{y,<\ell},C_{q}\right), (2)

where Yy=(Yy,1,…,Yy,|Yy|)Y_{y}=(Y_{y,1},\ldots,Y_{y,|Y_{y}|}) denotes the token sequence of entity yy under the tokenizer vocabulary 𝒲\mathcal{W}. During inference, the generation space is constrained to valid entity names in ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Structure-Semantic Collaborative Alignment

A central difficulty in generative MKGR is that graph topology and language semantics are represented in fundamentally different spaces. To bridge this gap, NaviGATE first learns structure-aware entity representations and aligns them with textual semantic representations.

Structure-aware entity encoding.

We use a graph encoder fg​(⋅)f_{g}(\cdot) to encode each entity into a structure-aware representation. For entity eie_{i}, its representation is obtained by aggregating information from its local neighborhood 𝒩i\mathcal{N}_{i}:

𝐬i=σ⁡(∑j∈𝒩i∪{i}αi​j​𝐖g​𝐱j),\mathbf{s}_{i}=\sigma\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}\cup\{i\}}\alpha_{ij}\mathbf{W}_{g}\mathbf{x}_{j}\bigr), (3)

where 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j} is the initial feature of entity eje_{j}, 𝐖g\mathbf{W}_{g} is a learnable transformation matrix, αi​j\alpha_{ij} is the attention weight between eie_{i} and eje_{j}, and σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is a activation function.

To preserve relational geometry, we further impose a translation-based structural objective (Bordes et al. 2013b). For each positive triple (h,r,t)∈𝒯(h,r,t)\in\mathcal{T}, we construct a corrupted negative triple (h¯,r,t¯)(\bar{h},r,\bar{t}) by replacing either the head or the tail entity. The structural loss is defined as

ℒkg=∑(h,r,t)∈𝒯[γ+d⁡(𝐬h+𝐫,𝐬t)−d⁡(𝐬h¯+𝐫,𝐬t¯)]+.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{kg}}=\sum_{(h,r,t)\in\mathcal{T}}\left[\gamma+d(\mathbf{s}_{h}+\mathbf{r},\mathbf{s}_{t})-d(\mathbf{s}_{\bar{h}}+\mathbf{r},\mathbf{s}_{\bar{t}})\right]_{+}. (4)

where 𝐫\mathbf{r} denotes the relation embedding, d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) is implemented as the L1L_{1} distance, γ\gamma is the margin, and [x]+=max⁡(0,x)[x]_{+}=\max(0,x). This objective encourages valid triples to have lower energy than corrupted triples, thereby preserving graph topology in the structural embedding space.

Contrastive structure–text alignment.

Although 𝐬i\mathbf{s}_{i} captures graph topology, it resides in a geometry-driven space that is misaligned with the semantic space of language models. To bridge this gap, we ground the structural representation of each entity in its textual semantics. Concretely, we encode the entity description did_{i} with a frozen language encoder to obtain the textual representation 𝐮i\mathbf{u}_{i}, and map both representations into a shared space:

𝐬¯i=Norm⁡(gs​(𝐬i)),𝐮¯i=Norm⁡(gt​(𝐮i)),\bar{\mathbf{s}}_{i}=\mathrm{Norm}\left(g_{s}(\mathbf{s}_{i})\right),\quad\bar{\mathbf{u}}_{i}=\mathrm{Norm}\left(g_{t}(\mathbf{u}_{i})\right), (5)

where gs​(⋅)g_{s}(\cdot) and gt​(⋅)g_{t}(\cdot) are learnable projection heads, and Norm⁡(⋅)\mathrm{Norm}(\cdot) denotes L2L_{2} normalization.

We adopt a symmetric contrastive objective to align matched graph-text pairs while separating mismatched pairs within the same mini-batch. Let ℬ\mathcal{B} denote a mini-batch, and define the InfoNCE loss as

ℓNCE​(𝐚i,𝐛i)=−log⁡exp⁡(sim⁡(𝐚i,𝐛i)/τ)∑j∈ℬexp⁡(sim⁡(𝐚i,𝐛j)/τ),\ell_{\mathrm{NCE}}(\mathbf{a}_{i},\mathbf{b}_{i})=-\log\frac{\exp\left(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{a}_{i},\mathbf{b}_{i})/\tau\right)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{B}}\exp\left(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{a}_{i},\mathbf{b}_{j})/\tau\right)}, (6)

where sim⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathrm{sim}(\cdot,\cdot) denotes cosine similarity and τ\tau is a temperature parameter. The symmetric graph-text contrastive loss is written in expectation form as

ℒcon=12​𝔼i∼ℬ​[ℓNCE​(𝐬¯i,𝐮¯i)+ℓNCE​(𝐮¯i,𝐬¯i)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{i\sim\mathcal{B}}\left[\ell_{\mathrm{NCE}}\left(\bar{\mathbf{s}}_{i},\bar{\mathbf{u}}_{i}\right)+\ell_{\mathrm{NCE}}\left(\bar{\mathbf{u}}_{i},\bar{\mathbf{s}}_{i}\right)\right]. (7)

The overall alignment objective is

ℒalign=ℒkg+λcon​ℒcon,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{kg}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{con}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}}, (8)

where λcon\lambda_{\mathrm{con}} balances the contributions of the structural and contrastive objectives.

Structure-Aware Internal Knowledge Activation

Retrieval-augmented methods depend heavily on the quality of the retrieved candidate set. However, in realistic MKGR scenarios, the ground-truth entity may be absent due to limited retriever recall. To reduce such over-dependence on retrieval, NaviGATE first activates the model’s retrieval-free completion ability before exposing it to retrieved candidates.

Query-aware multimodal entity summarization.

Raw entity descriptions, images, and neighboring triples can be lengthy, redundant, and noisy. Directly concatenating them into the prompt may cause context dilution and make it difficult for the MLLM to identify query-relevant evidence. Therefore, for each entity ee involved in query qq, we construct a compact query-aware multimodal summary:

Seq=Summarize⁡(q,de,ie,𝒩e),S_{e}^{q}=\mathrm{Summarize}\left(q,d_{e},i_{e},\mathcal{N}_{e}\right), (9)

where ded_{e} is the textual description, iei_{e} is the associated image, and 𝒩e\mathcal{N}_{e} denotes the local structural neighborhood of ee. The summary SeS_{e} converts heterogeneous evidence into a concise textual form, highlighting entity attributes, visual cues, and graph-neighborhood semantics relevant to query.

Structural token injection.

To explicitly provide the MLLM with graph structural information, we project the aligned structural representation into the input embedding space of the MLLM. Specifically, for each entity ee, we compute

𝐩e=ϕ⁡(𝐬e),\mathbf{p}_{e}=\phi(\mathbf{s}_{e}), (10)

where ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) is a lightweight multilayer perceptron that matches the dimension of 𝐬e\mathbf{s}_{e} to that of the MLLM token embeddings. The projected vector 𝐩e\mathbf{p}_{e} is treated as a soft structural token and inserted into the input embedding sequence.

For a tail prediction query q=(h,r,∗)q=(h,r,\ast) as an example, the retrieval-free context is constructed as

Cqfree=Prompt⁡(q,Shq,𝐩h),C_{q}^{\mathrm{free}}=\mathrm{Prompt}\left(q,S_{h}^{q},\mathbf{p}_{h}\right), (11)

where ShqS_{h}^{q} provides query-aware multimodal evidence for the observed entity, while 𝐩h\mathbf{p}_{h} encodes its structural context. The context excludes retrieved candidate entities, encouraging the model to predict the missing entity based on its internal parametric knowledge and the provided multimodal and structural evidence.

Retrieval-free warm-up objective.

The model is optimized to generate the ground-truth entity name from the retrieval-free context:

ℒact=−∑ℓ=1|Yy|logPθ(Yy,ℓ∣Yy,<ℓ,Cqfree).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}=-\sum_{\ell=1}^{|Y_{y}|}\log P_{\theta}\left(Y_{y,\ell}\mid Y_{y,<\ell},C_{q}^{\mathrm{free}}\right). (12)

This stage equips the model with retrieval-independent completion ability by learning to predict the missing entity from its parametric knowledge and the provided multimodal-structural evidence. It also establishes a retrieval-free prediction distribution that later serves as a stable reference for suppressing misleading candidate evidence.

Noise-Aware Dual-View Instruction Tuning

Building on the retrieval-free completion ability established during internal knowledge activation, NaviGATE is further optimized with retrieved candidates. Let 𝒦q=k1,…,kK\mathcal{K}_{q}={k_{1},\ldots,k_{K}} denote the top-K candidate entities retrieved for query qq by an embedding-based retriever. These candidates may provide useful non-parametric evidence, but the ground-truth entity may be absent and the remaining candidates may be misleading. Therefore, the model should learn to exploit retrieved evidence when it is reliable, while preserving its internal parametric knowledge when retrieval is noisy.

To this end, we construct two complementary views for each training query:

Cqfree\displaystyle C_{q}^{\mathrm{free}} =Prompt⁡(q,Sh,𝐩h),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Prompt}(q,S_{h},\mathbf{p}_{h}), (13)
Cqaware\displaystyle C_{q}^{\mathrm{aware}} =Prompt⁡(q,Sh,𝐩h,𝒦q).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Prompt}(q,S_{h},\mathbf{p}_{h},\mathcal{K}_{q}).

The retrieval-free view captures the model’s internal belief without external candidates, while the retrieval-aware view incorporates retrieved entity evidence.

Let Yy=(Yy,1,…,Yy,|Yy|)Y_{y}=(Y_{y,1},\ldots,Y_{y,|Y_{y}|}) denote the token sequence of the ground-truth entity. At each decoding position ℓ\ell, under teacher forcing with prefix Yy,<ℓY_{y,<\ell}, the model produces vocabulary logits for each view:

𝐳θ,ℓv=LMHead⁡(𝐡θ,ℓv)∈ℝ|𝒱|,v∈{free,aware},\mathbf{z}_{\theta,\ell}^{v}=\operatorname{LMHead}\left(\mathbf{h}_{\theta,\ell}^{v}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|},\quad v\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{aware}\}, (14)

where 𝐡θ,ℓv\mathbf{h}_{\theta,\ell}^{v} is the hidden state conditioned on context CqvC_{q}^{v} and prefix Yy,<ℓY_{y,<\ell}, and 𝒱\mathcal{V} denotes the vocabulary.

Sharpened generative supervision for reliable retrieval.


When the ground-truth entity is included in the retrieved set, i.e., y∈𝒦qy\in\mathcal{K}_{q}, the retrieved candidates provide useful external evidence. In this case, the retrieval-aware logits should be encouraged to amplify the preference gain induced by the retrieved context.

Specifically, for each decoding position ℓ\ell, we first compute the retrieval-induced logit shift:

Δ​𝐳θ,ℓ=𝐳θ,ℓaware−sg⁡[𝐳θ,ℓfree],\Delta\mathbf{z}_{\theta,\ell}=\mathbf{z}_{\theta,\ell}^{\mathrm{aware}}-\operatorname{sg}\left[\mathbf{z}_{\theta,\ell}^{\mathrm{free}}\right], (15)

where sg⁡[⋅]\operatorname{sg}[\cdot] denotes the stop-gradient operation. We then construct sharpened retrieval-aware logits:

𝐳~θ,ℓ=𝐳θ,ℓaware+ϵ​Δ​𝐳θ,ℓ,\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\theta,\ell}=\mathbf{z}_{\theta,\ell}^{\mathrm{aware}}+\epsilon\Delta\mathbf{z}_{\theta,\ell}, (16)

where ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0 controls the sharpening strength. Equivalently,

𝐳~θ,ℓ=(1+ϵ)​𝐳θ,ℓaware−ϵ​sg⁡[𝐳θ,ℓfree].\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\theta,\ell}=(1+\epsilon)\mathbf{z}_{\theta,\ell}^{\mathrm{aware}}-\epsilon\operatorname{sg}\left[\mathbf{z}_{\theta,\ell}^{\mathrm{free}}\right]. (17)

This operation amplifies the logit-level preference shift from the retrieval-free view to the retrieval-aware view, thereby strengthening the useful signal introduced by reliable retrieval.

The reliable-retrieval loss is computed as the token-level negative log-likelihood under the sharpened logits:

ℒrel=−1|Yy|∑ℓ=1|Yy|logexp⁡(z~θ,ℓ,Yy,ℓ)∑w∈𝒱exp⁡(z~θ,ℓ,w).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}=-\frac{1}{|Y_{y}|}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|Y_{y}|}\log\frac{\exp\left(\widetilde{z}_{\theta,\ell,Y_{y,\ell}}\right)}{\sum_{w\in\mathcal{V}}\exp\left(\widetilde{z}_{\theta,\ell,w}\right)}. (18)

This objective encourages the model to enlarge the relative advantage of the ground-truth entity under the retrieval-aware view, while suppressing candidate preferences that mainly originate from the retrieval-free prior.

Parametric consistency distillation for noisy retrieval.

When the ground-truth entity is absent from the retrieved set, i.e., y∉𝒦qy\notin\mathcal{K}_{q}, applying logit sharpening to the retrieval-aware prediction may bias the model toward plausible but incorrect candidates. Therefore, we use the retrieval-free branch as a parametric anchor and constrain the retrieval-aware branch at each decoding position.

For each output position ℓ\ell, we minimize the KL divergence between the retrieval-free token distribution and the retrieval-aware token distribution:

ℒpcd\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pcd}} =1|Yy|​∑ℓ=1|Yy|DKL​(sg⁡[𝐩θ,ℓfree]∥𝐩θ,ℓaware)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|Y_{y}|}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|Y_{y}|}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\operatorname{sg}\left[\mathbf{p}_{\theta,\ell}^{\mathrm{free}}\right]\,\middle\|\,\mathbf{p}_{\theta,\ell}^{\mathrm{aware}}\right) (19)
=1|Yy|​∑ℓ=1|Yy|∑w∈𝒱sg⁡[pθ,ℓ,wfree]​log⁡sg⁡[pθ,ℓ,wfree]pθ,ℓ,waware,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|Y_{y}|}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|Y_{y}|}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{V}}\operatorname{sg}\left[p_{\theta,\ell,w}^{\mathrm{free}}\right]\log\frac{\operatorname{sg}\left[p_{\theta,\ell,w}^{\mathrm{free}}\right]}{p_{\theta,\ell,w}^{\mathrm{aware}}},

where

𝐩θ,ℓv=softmax⁡(𝐳θ,ℓv),v∈{free,aware}.\mathbf{p}_{\theta,\ell}^{v}=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\mathbf{z}_{\theta,\ell}^{v}\right),\quad v\in\{\mathrm{free},\mathrm{aware}\}. (20)

The stop-gradient operation prevents the consistency objective from updating the retrieval-free branch, while encouraging the retrieval-aware branch to resist misleading retrieval evidence and remain consistent with the model’s internal parametric knowledge. Finally, the dual-view tuning objective is

ℒdual=𝕀[y∈𝒦q]ℒrel+λk​l𝕀[y∉𝒦q]ℒpcd,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dual}}=\mathbb{I}\left[y\in\mathcal{K}_{q}\right]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}+\lambda_{kl}\mathbb{I}\left[y\notin\mathcal{K}_{q}\right]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pcd}}, (21)

where λk​l\lambda_{kl} balances the parametric consistency objective.

Structure-Constrained Inference

Unconstrained generation may produce entity names that do not exist in the target knowledge graph. Since MKGR requires each prediction to correspond to a valid entity in ℰ\mathcal{E}, we introduce a structure-constrained decoding strategy to ensure entity validity.

We first construct a prefix trie 𝒫\mathcal{P} from the tokenized names of all entities in ℰ\mathcal{E}, with an end-of-sequence token appended to each entity name. At decoding step tt, given the generated prefix Y<tY_{<t}, the set of valid next tokens is defined as

Ω⁡(Y<t)={w∈𝒱|Y<t∘w​ is a valid prefix in ​𝒫},\Omega(Y_{<t})=\left\{w\in\mathcal{V}\;\middle|\;Y_{<t}\circ w\text{ is a valid prefix in }\mathcal{P}\right\}, (22)

where ∘\circ denotes token concatenation. We then define the vocabulary constraint mask as

Mt​(w)={0,w∈Ω⁡(Y<t),−∞,w∉Ω⁡(Y<t).M_{t}(w)=\begin{cases}0,&w\in\Omega(Y_{<t}),\\ -\infty,&w\notin\Omega(Y_{<t}).\end{cases} (23)

During inference, NaviGATE computes the retrieval-free and retrieval-aware token logits, denoted by 𝐳θ,tfree\mathbf{z}_{\theta,t}^{\mathrm{free}} and 𝐳θ,taware\mathbf{z}_{\theta,t}^{\mathrm{aware}}, respectively. Both predictions are conditioned on the generated prefix Y<tY_{<t}. We define the retrieval-induced logit shift as

Δ​𝐳θ,t=𝐳θ,taware−𝐳θ,tfree.\Delta\mathbf{z}_{\theta,t}=\mathbf{z}_{\theta,t}^{\mathrm{aware}}-\mathbf{z}_{\theta,t}^{\mathrm{free}}. (24)

Following the logit-level adjustment used during training, the inference logits are computed as

𝐳~θ,t=𝐳θ,taware+η​Δ​𝐳θ,t,\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\theta,t}=\mathbf{z}_{\theta,t}^{\mathrm{aware}}+\eta\Delta\mathbf{z}_{\theta,t}, (25)

where η≥0\eta\geq 0 controls the adjustment strength. The final decoding distribution is defined as

Pθ​(Yt=w∣Y<t,q)=exp⁡(z~θ,t,w+Mt​(w))∑v∈𝒱exp⁡(z~θ,t,v+Mt​(v)).P_{\theta}\left(Y_{t}=w\mid Y_{<t},q\right)=\frac{\exp\left(\widetilde{z}_{\theta,t,w}+M_{t}(w)\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\exp\left(\widetilde{z}_{\theta,t,v}+M_{t}(v)\right)}. (26)

The prefix constraint ensures that each completed output corresponds to a valid entity name in the target KG. When retrieved candidates provide useful evidence, the logit adjustment strengthens the retrieval-induced preference. Under noisy retrieval, parametric consistency distillation reduces the discrepancy between the retrieval-free and retrieval-aware predictions, thereby limiting the influence of misleading candidates.

Experiments

Experimental Setup

Datasets.

We evaluate NaviGATE on two widely used multimodal knowledge graph reasoning benchmarks, namely DB15K and MKG-W. DB15K contains 12,842 entities, 279 relations, 79,222 training triples, 9,902 validation triples, and 9,904 test triples. MKG-W contains 15,000 entities, 169 relations, 34,196 training triples, 4,276 validation triples, and 4,274 test triples. Both datasets provide structural triples together with multimodal entity information, making them suitable for evaluating the ability of MKGR models.

Baselines.

We compare NaviGATE with three categories of baseline methods. First, we include representative unimodal knowledge graph embedding models that rely only on structural triples, including TransE (Bordes et al. 2013a), DistMult (Yang et al. 2015), ComplEx (Trouillon et al. 2016), RotatE (Sun et al. 2019), and TuckER (Balazevic et al. 2019). Second, we compare with discriminative MKGR methods that incorporate visual or textual information into entity representation learning, including OTKGE (Cao et al. 2022), IMF (Li et al. 2023), QEB (Wang et al. 2023), AdaMF (Zhang et al. 2024d), SnAg (Chen et al. 2025), NativE (Zhang et al. 2024a), MyGO (Zhang et al. 2025), and APKGR (Jian et al. 2025). Third, we include generation-based KGR methods, including DIFT (Liu et al. 2025a) and SAT (Liu et al. 2025b), to evaluate whether NaviGATE can leverage generative reasoning while maintaining robustness to noisy retrieval results.

Implementation Details.

We conduct all experiments on an Intel Xeon Gold CPU with 4 NVIDIA 4090 GPUs, each with 24 GB memory, under Ubuntu 18.04 LTS. We select TuckER and RotatE as representative embedding-based retrievers. Each retriever is first pretrained on the training set, and the top-20 predicted entities are then retrieved for each query as candidate entities. For the multimodal generative backbone, we use Qwen3-VL 8B as the base model and adopt LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) for parameter-efficient finetuning. The LoRA rank, scaling factor, and dropout rate are set to 64, 16, and 0.1, respectively. We train the model for 2 epochs in the internal knowledge activation stage and 4 epochs in the dual-view instruction tuning stage. During inference, we use prefix-trie constrained decoding to generate a valid entity, place it at the top of the retriever’s original ranking, remove any duplicate occurrence, and preserve the relative order of all remaining entities. We then report standard filtered MRR and Hits@1/3/10.

Main Results.

Table 1 reports the overall results. Compared with unimodal KGR methods, NaviGATE consistently achieves better performance on both datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of integrating multimodal information with generative reasoning for MKGR.

Compared with discriminative MKGR baselines, NaviGATE achieves stronger and more consistent performance on the key top-ranking metrics across both datasets. On MKG-W, NaviGATE+RotatE improves the best MRR and Hits@1 from 0.374 and 0.306 to 0.408 and 0.361, respectively, demonstrating a clear advantage in ranking the correct entity at the top. On DB15K, NaviGATE+TuckER reaches an MRR of 0.383 and a Hits@1 of 0.313, also surpassing the strongest discriminative baselines.

Compared with LLM-based methods such as DIFT and SAT, NaviGATE achieves further improvements under both retrievers. On MKG-W, NaviGATE+RotatE improves MRR by 1.8 percentage points over DIFT+RotatE, while NaviGATE+TuckER outperforms SAT+TuckER by 1.5 percentage points. On DB15K, NaviGATE+TuckER further improves MRR by 1.4 percentage points over SAT+TuckER. These results show that noise-aware tuning effectively exploits reliable candidates while mitigating noisy retrieval.

Ablation Study.

Table 2 presents the ablation results on MKG-W. Removing stage-1 pretraining or the structural contrastive loss decreases MRR from 0.408 to 0.401 and 0.405, respectively, confirming that structure-semantic alignment provides a useful foundation for subsequent generative reasoning. In the dual-view tuning stage, removing stage-2 finetuning causes a substantial drop in both MRR and Hits@1, while removing the retrieval-aware branch results in the lowest Hits@1 of 0.248. These results indicate that retrieved evidence remains essential when properly incorporated through noise-aware optimization. The multimodal summary, structure-constrained decoding, KL loss, and retrieval-free branch also yield consistent improvements, demonstrating their complementary roles in semantic enrichment, valid entity generation, and robustness to noisy candidates. Among the three modalities, removing textual information leads to the largest degradation, whereas visual and structural information provide smaller but stable gains. To directly evaluate robustness under retrieval failure, we further report results on the subset where the ground-truth entity is absent from the candidate set. As shown in Table 2, NaviGATE improves Hits@1 by 1.1 percentage points over the variant without parametric consistency, confirming its ability to suppress misleading retrieval evidence.

Impact of the Number of Retrieved Candidates.

Figure 2 analyzes the effect of candidate number on MKG-W. Increasing candidates from 10 to 20 improves MRR from 0.391 to 0.408 and Hits@1 from 0.347 to 0.361, showing that a moderate candidate set provides more useful retrieval evidence. However, further increasing the number to 30 or 40 brings no additional gain and slightly degrades performance, likely due to more noisy distractors in the prompt. Since training time also increases steadily with more candidates, we use 20 candidates as the default setting for better accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity.

Figure 3 shows the sensitivity of NaviGATE to λk​l\lambda_{kl} and ε\varepsilon on MKG-W. For λk​l\lambda_{kl}, the model performs stably when it ranges from 0.01 to 0.5, while a larger value of 1.0 slightly degrades both MRR and Hits@1. This suggests that moderate parametric consistency helps suppress noisy retrieval, whereas overly strong regularization may limit the benefit of retrieval-aware evidence. For ε\varepsilon, the best performance is achieved around 0.2–0.5. A small ε\varepsilon provides insufficient logit sharpening, while a large value over-amplifies retrieval-induced shifts and introduces noise. Therefore, we set λk​l=0.1\lambda_{kl}=0.1 and ε=0.2\varepsilon=0.2 by default.

Case Study.

Figure 4 shows representative cases under different retrieval conditions. When the ground-truth entity appears in the candidate list, NaviGATE exploits retrieval evidence to generate the correct answer. More importantly, even when the ground-truth entity is absent from the candidates, NaviGATE can still recover it using activated internal knowledge. The failure cases further show that distinguishing highly confusable entities under ambiguous multimodal cues remains challenging, highlighting the inherent difficulty of noise-aware reasoning in MKGR.

Conclusion

In this paper, we propose NaviGATE, a noise-aware generative framework for multimodal knowledge graph reasoning. NaviGATE aligns structural representations with textual semantics, activates retrieval-free completion through multimodal summaries and structural token injection, and employs dual-view instruction tuning to exploit reliable candidates while suppressing misleading ones via parametric consistency. Structure-constrained decoding further ensures valid entity generation. Experiments demonstrate its effectiveness and robustness. In future work, we will extend NaviGATE to incorporate more modality information beyond text and images, and explore robust designs for missing-modality scenarios to improve real-world MKGR reliability.
